1:
The chapter is dated by the imprisonment it caused. John Gill, Matthew Henry and Charles Ellicott all note that this word was delivered while the prophet was at liberty and became the ground of his commitment, being quoted for that purpose later. Adam Clarke divides the chapter into two discourses, one during the siege and one after the Chaldeans had broken it off, and dates the first to the tenth year of the reign. Keil and Delitzsch concede that this chapter and the two following want any external bond of unity, report that several scholars have marked them as appendixes, and answer that the label accounts for neither their position nor their connection. Ellicott traces a later copyist in the spelling of the name here and in the piling up of nouns after it. John Calvin draws another inference: Zedekiah was not so proud and cruel as tyrants usually are, so the fury the prophet met must have come from the pride of the people, who made a mild king angry with him.

On the sentence Calvin fills in what happened. The king was taken in flight, carried to Riblah and tried as a criminal rather than as a king, saw his sons and counsellors killed before him, and was blinded and bound and brought to Babylon; the promise that his eyes should behold the eyes of his conqueror points, Calvin thinks, at just that. Henry meets the old objection with the same fact: another prophet had said he should not see Babylon, and he did not, for his eyes were put out. Calvin adds that though the revolt against a king who had set him on the throne was real ingratitude, the prophet looks past such causes; and that threatenings repeated to deaf ears are never wasted, since they take away the excuse of ignorance.

That he shall die in peace is read as mercy, and by one as tactics. Ellicott finds the tone comparatively mild and thinks the motive was to persuade the king to give up a useless resistance, since going to Babylon need not shut him out from ease and an honourable burial; a predecessor was imprisoned there, but that followed from obstinate resistance, which this king might avoid by timely submission. Gill takes it to mean on his bed and in friendship with the king of Babylon, and perhaps at peace with God, if he repented in captivity. Henry hopes the same, and says a man may die in a prison and yet die in peace, since it is better to live and die penitent in a prison than impenitent in a palace. Calvin turns it into a question, whether violent death deserves so much dread. He recalls the heathen commander who argued at supper that the best death is the sudden one and got it next day, and answers that a natural death is easier, since nature shrinks from bloodshed and sickness leaves time to consider the hand of God; yet for some, he grants, it is better to be killed than to lie raging on a bed.

The burnings divide Clarke and Ellicott outright. Clarke illustrates the verse from funeral piles heaped with scented wood among the Hindoos. Ellicott denies the practice to this people: spices were burnt as a mark of honour at a royal burial, but the Hebrews never adopted cremation and mostly embalmed their dead. Calvin argues from the promise that burial is a symbol of immortality, distinguishing men from beasts whose carcases are left to rot, then qualifies himself, since the wicked are often buried with pomp while the saints are torn by wild beasts. On the dirge, John Wesley and Henry report the form the Jews preserved, that Zedekiah drank the dregs of all the ages before him; Ellicott gets its force from the contrast with the prophecy that another king should be buried without any lament.
6:
The bare notice that the prophet delivered the message is made much of by three voices. John Gill observes that he kept back no part of what he was sent with, the threatening as well as the consolatory, and delivered the whole faithfully. Adam Clarke puts the cost of it in a sentence: he spoke these words at the hazard of his life, for Jeremiah feared God and had no other fear. John Calvin works the same point out at length. The messenger was unwelcome and the danger real, yet he did his office, knowing that God would not suffer the king to touch him except for some good; he deposited his life in the hand of God and offered himself as a sacrifice when he dared to threaten a king openly, which could not be done without giving offence, and the wrath of a king, as the proverb says, is a messenger of death. His firmness deserves praise, Calvin adds, because he feared no danger once he saw that God had laid a necessity on him.

The two cities named at the end of the passage are Ellicott’s ground, and he gives each a history. Charles Ellicott notes that both appear here for the first time in the book. Lachish was one of the strongest towns of the Amorites in the days of Joshua, standing in the lowland country; it was fortified by Rehoboam as a defence against the northern kingdom; a king of Judah took refuge there when a conspiracy drove him out of Jerusalem; and Sennacherib took it on his march from Assyria toward Egypt and made it his headquarters. Ellicott adds that a carved slab recovered from the Assyrian ruins depicts that siege and gives something like a ground-plan of the place, though its own site has not been identified with certainty, ruins of a similar name lying inland from Gaza. Azekah he calls less conspicuous in history, also in the lowland, named in the old conquest narratives, and remembered as the place between which and another town the Philistines encamped in the days of Saul; it too was fortified by Rehoboam, and its site is unascertained, though two early writers place it between Jerusalem and a town of the plain. Clarke says only that both were cities of Judah of considerable importance and had been strongly fortified by the same king.

Calvin reads the same verse as a piece of irony. The prophet says that these were the cities of Judah that were left, and Calvin asks how many the cities of Judah then were. Two, he answers. So the notice quietly exposes the vain confidence of a king who still thought he could beat the enemy while he was master of three towns and no more. The reason those three had not yet fallen is given in the verse itself, that they were fortified places; from which Calvin infers that the rest were taken without trouble or surrendered of their own accord. What he draws from it is a judgment on the king. Zedekiah was already stripped of his power and had not given up the ferocity of his mind, nor was he moved by the threatenings; and that, Calvin says, was extreme madness and a sign that his mind was alienated, since the hand of God was plainly stretched out against him and he still ran headlong on his own ruin like a wild beast that has no reason. Gill, who elsewhere fills out such details, adds only that the army had laid close siege to the city and still continued it.
8:
A new prophecy begins, and the voices place it differently. John Gill puts it after the king of Babylon had raised the siege and gone to meet the king of Egypt, and reports but rejects a Jewish dating two years before the siege began. Adam Clarke makes the interval a few days after the first discourse. Charles Ellicott supplies the setting at length. The law allowed no more than seven years of bondage for a freeborn Hebrew, extended in the later legislation as a kind of serfage to the next jubilee. The law had fallen into disuse, and Ellicott compares the nobles of Judah to those of Athens before Solon and Rome before the tribunes, using the law of debt to bring fellow citizens into slavery. He offers several motives: the pressure of the invasion, the wish for the ready service of freemen rather than the forced work of slaves, and perhaps the revival of the law that followed its discovery under Josiah; the step, he thinks, gave fresh energy to the defenders.

Whether the release was tied to a fixed year they disagree. Clarke takes it to be the sabbatical year, the seventh being the year of release. Gill knows that view and answers it: the sabbatical year released debts, not servants, since a man who had not served out his time was not freed by it. Ellicott leaves it open between a sabbatic year, a jubilee, and a simple reparation for past neglect, noting that the phrase proclaim liberty belongs to the language of the jubilee.

Matthew Henry gives the law its reasons. God had put honour on that nation and would have them keep the difference between it and others; and having brought them out of slavery himself, he would have them show a grateful sense of it by letting go those to whom their own houses were houses of bondage. From which he draws the rule that we must release as we are released, forgive as we are forgiven, and relieve as we are relieved. He is plain about why it was broken: worldly profit weighed more than the command, and a servant of seven years understood his work better than a new one; but against an express law of God no custom may be pleaded, and for this sin God brought them into servitude justly. On the reform he notes that the prophets had to tell them what stood in the book they would not read; that when the king and princes led, the people could not for shame hold back; and that what God binds us to by precept it is good to bind ourselves to by promise.

On the reversal John Calvin works the verbs. The word for hearing is used twice in different senses, first of simple hearing and then of obedience, and by saying that princes and people alike heard, the prophet takes away every plea of ignorance; each sinned the more gravely for having been taught, one who knows his master will being beaten with more stripes. He notes the answering pair in the next verse, that they turned and made their servants return, the turning being a change of purpose after some fear of God had been felt. He does not doubt they alleged an excuse, and says that whatever subtlety men contrive to cover oppression, God requires integrity and condemns all craftiness. Gill dates the relapse to the moment the siege lifted, and says it proves they were never hearty in the covenant. Clarke reads the timing otherwise, that they had agreed to free the servants at the end of the seventh year and recalled it when the year ran out. Ellicott ends where the prophet does, with men brought back under a bondage made bitterer by a taste of freedom, and remarks that his sympathies, like those of true prophets, were with the poor and the oppressed.
12:
The charge is laid by quoting the law, and Charles Ellicott says why it existed. The prophet takes as his text the statute that had been broken and reminds them how it was given: their fathers had just been brought out of a house of bondage, and this was part of the covenant, freedom given on one side and obedience promised on the other. They were never to forget the bitterness of that servitude, and were to make it a fundamental law that no Israelite should pass, except by his own choice, into a hopeless lifelong slavery. John Calvin reaches the same by his own argument. Who can claim dominion over others who is himself a servant? There is no dominion where there is no liberty; a man may be free without owning a servant, but none is a master unless he is free. The Israelites were in a miserable servitude when God stretched out his hand to them, so their liberty came of gratuitous mercy; and men brought out of prison had no leave to domineer over their brethren for ever, but only for a term.

The length of that term is the hardest point of grammar here, since the verse says at the end of seven years and then speaks of six years of service. John Gill answers that it means within the compass of seven years, as soon as the seventh had begun, the term being of the seventh year coming in and not going out, and cites a later authority. Ellicott says the same from the context, and adds that the sabbath-year was to bring its rest to the slave as well as the land. Calvin reports that but for two other places where the same words stand he would have followed two of the versions and read otherwise, and settles on the explanation of the Rabbins, that the word covers the commencing as well as the terminating end, which he calls the best account of it.

On the fathers who would not hear, Calvin fastens on the second clause. To say that they did not incline their ear is emphatic beside not hearkening, for a man may neglect what is said or fail to understand it, but to close the ears deliberately is hopeless obstinacy. He explains the original neglect without charity: the law was a privilege that ought to have won them, but every man grew addicted to his own advantage and a temporary servitude became perpetual. Ellicott finds the same long violation implied, and reads two passages of the older prophet as protests.

The brief obedience is commended and turned against them. Gill allows that they had for a moment turned from their fathers ways and acted the better part. Calvin says God commends the repentance precisely to show how detestable hypocrisy is, since a people who made a show of obeying and remanded their servants soon after were trifling with him. Ellicott presses the place: not an edict merely, nor a judgment in court, but princes and people meeting in the Temple and covenanting in the presence of God, so that breaking it was a sin against him as well as their brethren. On the pollution of the name they divide the ground. Adam Clarke says they made the covenant in his name and called him to witness it, then dishonoured it. Ellicott identifies the verb with the word used of profaning the name in false swearing, and concludes that they broke the third commandment as well as the eighth. Calvin agrees that perjury is allied to sacrilege, since nothing is more precious to God than truth; and while the name may be polluted by rashness, the worst pollution is turning truth into a lie. He adds that the men freed were not willing to go back, the verb meaning to subject and oppress, so that inhumanity was piled on perjury.
17:
The sentence turns the word liberty back on the men who used it, and all hear the irony. Adam Clarke says the prophet loves to show the conformity between a crime and its punishment: they proclaimed liberty and God bound the sword in its sheath; they revoked it, and he gave liberty to the sword, the pestilence and the famine, so that in the punishment they might read the offence. These three are often named together, he adds, because they produce one another. Charles Ellicott presses it further. They had refused to serve as the servants of Jehovah, in whose service alone their freedom lay, and so are given the emancipation they denied to others, set free from his service and therefore from his protection: they refused the obedience which was freedom, and shall have the freedom which is bondage. John Wesley gives the plain content: they shall fall by sword and famine and plague, and the survivors be slaves among many nations.

John Calvin finds the clause open to two constructions and takes both. Read as liberty granted them, it means God will have no more to do with them: go and enjoy your liberty, and become the prey of other masters. Nothing is more miserable than such a discharge, when God dismisses those whose patron he has been. Read with the particle in its other sense, it is liberty proclaimed against them, God giving sword and pestilence and famine leave to rule over a people who would not bear his own rule. Behind both he sets the rule that the proclamation God counts is the one carried into effect: with men a profession is enough, but God makes nothing of a false one.

The rite of the divided calf is described most fully by Clarke, in five stages: a calf offered in sacrifice, the body divided from end to end so that half the spinal marrow lay on each side, the halves laid opposite with a passage between, the parties entering from either end to meet in the middle and swear, adjudging themselves to death if they broke faith, and then a feast on the victim. That last stage, he observes, gives point to the threat that follows, their bodies being made food for birds and beasts. Wesley describes the same more briefly, the parts laid in the temple over against one another and the parties passing between, silently agreeing that God should cut them in pieces like the beast.

Where the rite came from, the two who ask differ. Ellicott calls it a survival from patriarchal times, pointing to the covenant with Abraham where a burning lamp passed between the pieces, and traces the symbolism far afield, in a Greek phrase meaning literally to cut an oath and in a Roman prayer that Jupiter would smite the people as the priest smote the victim. Calvin agrees on the origin and adds that the Macedonians observed the like when mustering an army, but distinguishes the western rite: the Romans killed a sow with a stone and did not divide it, while among the Orientals the victims were cut in two, with the execration that the perjurer might be so cut asunder. John Gill notes that the covenant is called the Lord because made in his name and before him as witness, and thinks the calf was probably sacrificed to him, which made him a party to it. Calvin takes the same view, that it is not the Law but an agreement into which the name of God was brought, as marriage is called a covenant of God; so a broken pledge wrongs God as well as men, a sacrilege more atrocious than theft or fraud. He ends on the use of such signs, meant to keep slothful men awake and move all their senses, and on a people who imprecated that death on themselves and broke faith anyway.
19:
The list of the guilty is read closely. John Gill separates the princes of Judah from those of Jerusalem, making the first those who presided over the country towns and had fled into the city for safety, and the second its own magistrates. On the eunuchs the two other voices disagree outright. Charles Ellicott takes the word literally: such men were mostly of alien birth and became proselytes on entering the royal service; their prominence shows that in Judah, as in Assyria, they held high place at court; and he supposes they had enriched themselves, like the princes, by lending money to poorer Israelites and then bringing them into bondage. John Calvin denies that emasculated men are meant at all. The word was a title of the chief men, rendered rulers by one version and princes by another, and belonged to attendants on royalty; a married man of the old history bore it. The classes are named, he thinks, so that men elevated in the world may not suppose themselves exempt; and the citizens because the royal residence and the sanctuary made them proudest of all.

Ellicott notices that the sentence is not level. Bodies left for the birds are the extremest penalty in this book, but what is said of the king and his princes is milder, probably because he, though too weak to stop the evil, had not been prominent in breaking the covenant and showed more willingness to hear the prophet. Calvin uses the verse to state a rule about the wicked: the Chaldeans had their own object and never meant to serve God, yet performed his work like hired men, and even the fury that made them shed blood without measure came of his secret influence. On the unburied bodies he is careful. It would be no real loss to lie unburied, since burial brings the dead no advantage, yet it is a sign of vengeance; and he meets the objection that this has befallen the best of servants by answering that temporal punishment falls alike on good and bad.

Why the besiegers had withdrawn two voices explain with different tempers. Adam Clarke states the fact: hearing of an Egyptian army coming to relieve the city, the king of Babylon raised the siege, went out and defeated them, the prophecy falling in that interval. Calvin explains the Egyptian motive without charity. There was an alliance, but the Egyptians had no great care for the Jews; they knew that once the Chaldeans had finished this war they would turn on Egypt, and judged it better to meet that army in company with the Jews than to fight it alone afterwards. The city exulted as though the danger were over, and Calvin derides the folly of taking a siege lifted for a season as a siege ended.

That the army will come back is put as a matter of command. Gill makes the Lord of hosts the general of that army, sending it away to try the inhabitants and bringing it back to press the siege harder. Calvin guards the word: God does not command openly, since the Chaldeans never purposed to obey him, but by a hidden providence, in the sense in which he commands diseases and the sword and the famine, Scripture teaching by such language that nothing can touch us except so far as God intends. Clarke records the outcome, that they returned, reinvested the city, took it after an obstinate defence and burned it, carrying the king and his princes away. Calvin closes on the symmetry he has traced throughout: having dealt perfidiously with their servants, men who thought themselves perpetually free were doomed to a servitude of their own. He adds that the prophet spared neither king nor princes, and that none are fit to bear rule in the Church unless they can reprove the highest as boldly as the lowest.
